title: Versioning & Backward Compatibility
objectives: Classify API changes as breaking or non-breaking for tolerant clients
Compare URI, header, and date versioning strategies
Run a deprecation protocol backed by telemetry before removing anything
body:
# Versioning & Backward Compatibility

## The problem
Your API has 40 client apps you cannot recompile. You need to rename a field, split an endpoint, drop a deprecated flag. Ship it naively and every client breaks on its next call. The craft is evolving the contract so old clients keep working while new ones get improvements - and knowing when a breaking change is worth the cost of a new version.

## Breaking vs non-breaking
Non-breaking (just ship it):
- Add an optional request field.
- Add a field to responses, assuming clients ignore unknown keys.
- Add a new endpoint, method, or response enum value at the end.
- Relax a validation rule or raise a limit.

Breaking (needs a plan):
- Remove or rename a field or endpoint.
- Change a field's type or its semantics.
- Make an optional field required.
- Add a new enum value when clients use exhaustive switches - surprisingly breaking in practice.

## Versioning strategies
- URI path: `POST /v2/orders`. Obvious in logs, cacheable per version, trivial routing. Cost: code forks per version.
- Header: `API-Version: 2`. Cleaner URLs, but invisible in a browser address bar and easy to forget.
- Date-based: `Stripe-Version: 2026-01-15`. Communicates intent and cadence well.

Pick one and stay consistent. For most teams URI versioning is the right boring choice.

## The tolerance principle
Servers should ignore fields they do not recognize, and clients should too. Then adding a response field is truly non-breaking even for strict old clients - and every server addition does not become an outage. Brittle clients that fail on unknown fields turn your additive release into their downtime.

## Deprecation protocol
1. Announce: changelog, email, dashboard banner.
2. Mark in the contract: `deprecated: true` on the operation or schema, plus a machine-readable `Sunset` header.
3. Migrate: emit `Deprecation` headers, and count who still calls old endpoints.
4. Remove: only after usage telemetry hits (near) zero - never on a calendar promise alone.

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Wed, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT
Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/v1-sunset>; rel="sunset"
```

## Decision framework
- Is the change additive? -> no version bump; ship with docs and a changelog entry.
- Is the break contained to clients you control? -> fix forward, skip a version.
- Public or multi-tenant with unknown clients? -> new major version in the path, run both until telemetry says the old one is dead.

## Best practices
- Version at the API surface level, not per endpoint.
- Keep old versions on life support: security fixes yes, new features no.
- Automate a breaking-change diff (oasdiff) in CI as the gate.
- Log API version and client id on every request to drive sunset decisions.

## Common mistakes
- Renaming `user_name` to `username` because it is just cosmetic - it is a breaking change.
- Adding a required request field and calling it non-breaking because the docs say so.
- Running three versions forever with no telemetry, doubling every bug.
- Never deprecating: v0 endpoints from 2019 still handling real traffic.

examples.name: sunset-headers.sh
examples.code:
# Detect who is still on v1: read the deprecation headers
curl -sD - https://api.example.com/v1/orders/42 -o /dev/null
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# Deprecation: true
# Sunset: Wed, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT
# Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/v1-sunset>; rel="sunset"

exercise.prompt: Implement breaking(oldSchema, newSchema): both arguments map field names to type names. Return a list of breaking changes - "removed: field" for fields present in the old schema but absent from the new one, and "type changed: field (old -> new)" when a surviving field changed type.
hints: Iterate the OLD schema's entries; additions in the new schema are not breaking.
A missing key in the new schema is a removal; a present key with a different type is a type change.
Renaming name to username is exactly a removal from the old schema's perspective.

questions.prompt: Which change is non-breaking for tolerant clients?
options: Changing a field type from string to integer
questions.explanation: Additive changes are safe when clients ignore unknown fields; renames, type changes, and removals all break consumers.

questions.prompt: Adding a new enum value to a status field can break clients because…
options: Clients with exhaustive switches over known values fail on the new value
questions.explanation: Strict clients that switch over every known value have no branch for the new one, so an additive change still breaks them.

questions.prompt: When should a v1 endpoint actually be removed?
options: On the announced date, regardless of usage
After a deprecation notice plus telemetry shows usage near zero
questions.explanation: Telemetry is the ground truth for who still depends on the old version; removing on a date alone guarantees outages for users you never heard of.
